text:
1. Raw Performance vs. Long-Term AI Investment
You're right that AMD RX 9000 series, especially the RX 9700 XT and RX 9800 XT, are offering very competitive raw performance per dollar right now, especially in rasterization. That’s why people are hyping them up against cards like the RTX 5070 or 5060 Ti — those newer NVIDIA cards don’t look like big generational leaps in traditional performance.

But here's the catch: NVIDIA isn’t playing just the "raw power" game anymore. They're going all-in on AI and software-defined features like DLSS 3, Frame Generation, Reflex, RTX Video Super Resolution, and possibly more to come. This is where your point shines:

“We cannot see performance of actual games. Nvidia can still win in the long run.”

Exactly — it's about future-proofing, and NVIDIA has been laying the groundwork for that for years.

2. DLSS vs FSR – Hardware-Accelerated AI Matters
DLSS is backed by dedicated Tensor Cores, while AMD’s FSR (even FSR 3 with frame gen) is software-based and doesn't rely on AI in the same way. That difference may not matter as much today, but as games become more graphically intense and rely more on AI-driven upscaling and frame synthesis, the lack of hardware acceleration could become a serious bottleneck for AMD.

DLSS has already proven itself in games like Cyberpunk 2077 and Alan Wake II, where it can massively boost performance with relatively minimal visual compromise — something FSR can’t always match.

3. Game Development Trends
Game developers are starting to design with DLSS 3 and Frame Gen in mind — particularly in ray tracing-heavy titles. This trend favors NVIDIA cards even if AMD's raw specs look stronger on paper. If devs optimize more for DLSS (and less for FSR), that will amplify NVIDIA’s lead.

4. Longevity Argument
In 2–3 years, it’s very plausible that NVIDIA’s AI ecosystem will scale better with newer game engines and rendering pipelines. That’s what happened with the RTX 20 and 30 series over time. DLSS matured. Games added support. Suddenly those cards aged better than people expected.

So TL;DR:
Yes, AMD has a current price/performance edge in raw rasterization.

But NVIDIA’s long-term bet on AI, hardware-accelerated features, and deep developer partnerships might pay off in a bigger way over time.

If you're planning to keep a card for several years, the value of DLSS, Frame Gen, and future AI features could absolutely outweigh the raw performance gap seen today.
